Brazil! Lovely. And how have you found it here, all things considered?
Sorry, I don't understand. Can you say that again, more slowly?
Of course. Did you like the city?

With children, that is not easy. Was it difficult?
A little. One day I was lost in the street, and I asked a man. And you? Are you here on vacation?
For work, I am afraid. But your English is very good. Have a safe trip home.

Good morning, and welcome to your last day with us. This message is for the guests who leave today. Check-out is at eleven, and if you need one more hour, just call the reception. You can leave your bags in the small room next to the desk, and take them in the afternoon. Breakfast is until ten, on the ground floor, and today we have fruit and warm bread. If you need a taxi to the airport, call us thirty minutes before, and remember that on Sunday the traffic is slow, so leave early. One last thing: please check the room before you go, because every week somebody leaves a passport or a phone in the safe. It is a long way back. Thank you for staying with us, and have a very good trip home.

And now our travel minute. This week we talked to families about the first trip abroad with small children, and one answer came back again and again. It was not the money, and it was not the flight. It was the language. One mother told us she did not go into a single shop in ten days, because she was afraid of the moment somebody asks a question. Our expert says the same thing every time: you do not need to understand every word. You need three sentences. The first one asks people to repeat. The second one asks them to speak more slowly. And the third one asks for help. With those three, she says, a person who knows two hundred words can travel anywhere in the world. And that is our travel minute. Have a good week.
